name: Health and Nutrition
description: A comprehensive exploration of nutrition science covering macronutrients, micronutrients, hydration, dietary guidelines, sports nutrition, and global food systems for healthy adolescent lifestyles.

modules.title: Introduction to Nutrition
modules.objectives: Define nutrition and its importance to health, identify the six classes of nutrients, and use current federal dietary guidance to evaluate balanced, nutrient-dense food choices.
modules.readingNote: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services — current Dietary Guidelines for Americans and supporting resources.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 1: Introduction to Nutrition lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Review the current federal dietary guidance and identify two principles that could improve the provided or fictional food diary.
modules.assignment: Submit: an annotated three-day food diary and short explanation using provided, fictional, or anonymized data. Include: nutrient strengths, nutrient gaps, two realistic improvements, and citations to current federal guidance; calories, weight, diagnoses, and sensitive health details are not required. Evaluation: claims use specific diary evidence and accurately apply the six nutrient classes and nutrient-dense food guidance.

modules.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates
modules.titleZh: 宏量营养素：碳水化合物
modules.objectives: Identify types of carbohydrates (simple vs. complex, fiber), understand their role as the body's primary energy source, and evaluate healthy carbohydrate food choices.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Carbohydrates
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 2: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Carbohydrates and Blood Sugar; use the glycemic-index definition and its limits, then compare a provided or fictional food list without labeling foods morally as good or bad.
modules.assignment: Submit: a comparison report on simple and complex carbohydrate food sources. Include: the glycemic-index concept and its limits, fiber's role, three practical food swaps, and evidence from at least one qualified source. Evaluation: comparisons are accurate, each swap is justified, and the report avoids labeling single foods as universally good or bad.

modules.title: Macronutrients: Proteins
modules.objectives: Explain protein functions and essential amino acids, compare varied animal and plant protein sources, and explain why needs vary with age, body size, activity, growth, and health context.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — The Nutrition Source: Protein
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 3: Macronutrients: Proteins lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Compare two fictional meal patterns for protein variety and essential-amino-acid coverage; personal weight, intake targets, and medical information are not required.
modules.assignment: Submit: a calculation sheet and one-day meal plan for this fictional profile: a 15-year-old who weighs 60 kg, participates in moderate school activity, has no stated medical condition, and eats a mixed diet. Include: a reasonable protein range from a qualified cited source, calculation steps, an explanation of why individual needs vary, and varied food sources; this is an academic estimate, not a personal prescription. Evaluation: the calculation is traceable, the source is credible, and the meal plan reasonably fits the profile and module concepts.

modules.title: Macronutrients: Fats
modules.objectives: Classify dietary fats (saturated, unsaturated, trans), understand their health implications, and identify food sources of healthy fats. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Fats and Cholesterol
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 4: Macronutrients: Fats lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Analyze a food label for fat content and classify fats found in the product
modules.assignment: Submit: a practical guide to saturated, unsaturated, and trans fats. Include: definitions, food-source examples, health effects, and three justified substitutions that favor unsaturated fats when appropriate. Evaluation: the guide uses accurate course evidence, distinguishes fat types clearly, and gives realistic advice without recommending elimination of all dietary fat.

modules.title: Micronutrients: Vitamins
modules.objectives: Identify water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamins, their functions, food sources, and consequences of deficiency or excess. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamins and Minerals
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 5: Micronutrients: Vitamins lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Choose two vitamins from the NIH ODS fact-sheet collection and summarize their functions, food sources, deficiency risks, and upper-limit or excess cautions without diagnosing a person.
modules.assignment: Submit: a reference chart for four fat-soluble and four water-soluble vitamins. Include: major functions, several food sources, age-appropriate intake guidance from qualified sources, and risks of deficiency or excessive supplementation. Evaluation: all eight entries cite qualified evidence, categories are accurate, and the chart does not diagnose deficiencies or prescribe supplements.

modules.title: Micronutrients: Minerals
modules.objectives: Identify key dietary minerals (calcium, iron, potassium, sodium, zinc), their roles in body function, deficiency conditions, and food sources. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Minerals
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 6: Micronutrients: Minerals lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Use NIH ODS fact sheets to compare calcium and iron needs for a fictional adolescent profile; do not assess a real student or recommend supplements.
modules.assignment: Submit: a comparison of calcium, iron, and zinc for adolescent health. Include: functions, varied food sources, age-appropriate intake guidance from qualified sources, and consequences of inadequate or excessive intake. Evaluation: each mineral claim cites qualified evidence, individual needs are acknowledged, and no personal diagnosis or supplement prescription is made.

modules.title: Water & Hydration
modules.objectives: Explain water's roles in the body, understand daily hydration requirements, and recognize signs of dehydration and overhydration. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Water
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 7: Water & Hydration lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Analyze a fictional three-day fluid log and explain how activity, climate, foods, medicines, and health conditions can change hydration needs; avoid one universal intake target.
modules.assignment: Submit: a one-page hydration guide for a fictional teenager. Include: water's roles, factors that change fluid needs, early warning signs, a plan for routine activity, and when symptoms require adult or medical help. Evaluation: guidance is evidence-based, avoids one fixed target for everyone, and distinguishes routine hydration from special exercise or health needs.

modules.title: Energy Balance & Weight Management
modules.objectives: Explain energy balance and basal metabolic rate, evaluate growth-supporting approaches to health and weight, and recognize when a teenager should seek guidance from a parent, guardian, or qualified health professional.
modules.readingNote: CDC — Tips to Support Healthy Routines for Children and Teens; focus on growth-supporting food, activity, sleep, and family routines rather than a weight target.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 8: Energy Balance & Weight Management lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: NCBI Bookshelf — Energy: use its definition of basal metabolic rate and discussion of energy expenditure, then use NIDDK teen guidance at https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/take-charge-health-guide-teenagers for growth-supporting routines and qualified support. BMR is only one component of total energy needs; do not calculate a personal calorie target.
modules.assignment: Submit: a one-page analysis of this fictional media claim: ‘Every teenager can safely lose weight by eating exactly 1,200 calories a day because everyone has the same metabolism.’ Include: an accurate BMR definition, factors that make energy needs vary, evidence about adolescent growth and sustainability, growth-supporting alternatives, and when a parent, guardian, pediatrician, or registered dietitian should be consulted. Use the assigned CDC, NCBI Bookshelf, and NIDDK resources; personal weight or calorie targets are not required. Evaluation: the analysis identifies the claim's errors and risks, cites qualified-source evidence, and proposes safe, realistic alternatives.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six classes of nutrients?
options: Enzymes
Minerals
Carbohydrates
Vitamins
quizQuestions.answer: Enzymes
quizQuestions.explanation: The six classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water. Enzymes are biological catalysts, not a nutrient class.

quizQuestions.question: Which nutrient class provides the most calories per gram?
options: Protein
Vitamins
Carbohydrates
Fat
quizQuestions.answer: Fat
quizQuestions.explanation: Fat provides 9 calories per gram, compared to 4 calories per gram for both carbohydrates and protein.

quizQuestions.question: Which nutrient supports fluid balance and temperature regulation without providing calories?
options: Water
Carbohydrate
Fat
Protein
quizQuestions.answer: Water
quizQuestions.explanation: Water is an essential nutrient that supports transport, temperature regulation, and fluid balance but does not provide calories.

quizQuestions.question: Why is good nutrition especially important during adolescence?
quizQuestions.answer: Good nutrition supports rapid growth, brain development, energy, immune function, learning, activity, and long-term health patterns during adolescence.
quizQuestions.explanation: Adolescence is a major period of physical and cognitive development, so food quality affects both daily function and future health.

quizQuestions.question: Which food choice best represents a high-quality carbohydrate source for steady energy?
options: A bowl of sweetened refined-grain breakfast cereal
A bowl of oatmeal topped with chopped fresh fruit
A glass of fruit juice with a low-fiber snack bar
A plate of refined crackers with a sweet spread
quizQuestions.answer: A bowl of oatmeal topped with chopped fresh fruit
quizQuestions.explanation: High-quality carbohydrate sources provide energy along with fiber and nutrients, which support steadier blood sugar and longer-lasting fuel.

quizQuestions.question: Dietary fiber is best described as:
options: A carbohydrate stored chiefly in muscle and liver
A carbohydrate quickly broken down into glucose
A carbohydrate not fully digested by human enzymes
A carbohydrate absorbed intact through the intestine
quizQuestions.answer: A carbohydrate not fully digested by human enzymes
quizQuestions.explanation: Dietary fiber includes carbohydrates that human digestive enzymes do not fully break down. Different fibers support bowel function, satiety, and blood-glucose regulation; some are fermented by gut microbes.

quizQuestions.question: What does the glycemic index compare under standardized test conditions?
options: Added-sugar amounts in equal-weight food portions
Carbohydrate amounts in customary serving portions
Nutrient density relative to each food’s energy content
Glucose responses to matched carbohydrate portions
quizQuestions.answer: Glucose responses to matched carbohydrate portions
quizQuestions.explanation: The glycemic index compares blood-glucose responses to standardized portions containing equal amounts of available carbohydrate. It does not measure usual serving size, nutrient density, or a food’s overall health value.

quizQuestions.question: What is the primary function of carbohydrates in the body?
options: Regulating fluid balance between cells
Supplying amino acids for tissue growth and repair
Helping the absorption of fat-soluble dietary vitamins
Providing fuel for brain activity and exercise
quizQuestions.answer: Providing fuel for brain activity and exercise
quizQuestions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the body's preferred energy source, especially for brain function and moderate-to-high intensity exercise.

quizQuestions.question: A complete protein contains:
options: A high protein content despite amino-acid imbalances
A protein mixture that comes exclusively from animal foods
All nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions
Essential amino acids made by the body from other nutrients
quizQuestions.answer: All nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions
quizQuestions.explanation: A complete protein provides all nine essential amino acids that the body cannot synthesize on its own.

quizQuestions.question: Which food source provides complete protein?
options: Lentils
Black beans
Brown rice
Eggs
quizQuestions.answer: Eggs
quizQuestions.explanation: Eggs supply all nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions. Lentils, black beans, and brown rice also contain essential amino acids, but have lower proportions of one or more; varied plant foods can meet protein needs across the day.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement about protein needs for active teenagers is most accurate?
options: Needs reflect growth, body size, activity, health, and diet
Needs chiefly reflect whether protein comes from supplements
Needs chiefly reflect height rather than growth or activity
Needs follow a fixed target shared by active adolescents
quizQuestions.answer: Needs reflect growth, body size, activity, health, and diet
quizQuestions.explanation: Qualified guidance considers the whole person and diet rather than applying one universal target.

quizQuestions.question: How can a vegetarian eating pattern provide all essential amino acids?
quizQuestions.answer: A varied vegetarian pattern can meet essential amino-acid needs through foods such as beans, lentils, soy, dairy or eggs when included, nuts, seeds, and grains across the day.
quizQuestions.explanation: Most students do not need to combine complementary proteins in the same meal; variety and adequate total intake across the day matter.

quizQuestions.question: Which group generally supplies more saturated fat than the other listed groups?
options: Butter, fatty beef, and full-fat cheese
Sunflower oil, canola oil, and almonds
Salmon, walnuts, and ground flaxseed
Olive oil, avocado, and unsalted peanuts
quizQuestions.answer: Butter, fatty beef, and full-fat cheese
quizQuestions.explanation: Saturated fats are abundant in animal products like butter, red meat, and full-fat dairy, and are linked to elevated LDL cholesterol.

quizQuestions.question: Which blood-cholesterol pattern helps explain the cardiovascular risk of industrial trans fats?
options: Lower LDL and HDL cholesterol together
Raise LDL and lower HDL cholesterol
Raise HDL without affecting LDL cholesterol
Lower LDL without affecting HDL cholesterol
quizQuestions.answer: Raise LDL and lower HDL cholesterol
quizQuestions.explanation: Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL cholesterol, significantly increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease.

quizQuestions.question: Which role is associated with omega-3 fatty acids?
options: Supporting heart and brain function
Providing rapid fuel for sprints
Serving as building blocks for muscle proteins
Storing glucose for rapid release during exercise
quizQuestions.answer: Supporting heart and brain function
quizQuestions.explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids help support cell membranes and normal heart and brain function. Carbohydrates are the main rapid fuel for high-intensity activity, amino acids form proteins, and glycogen stores glucose.

quizQuestions.question: Which substitution replaces a source richer in saturated fat with one richer in unsaturated fat?
options: Replace olive oil with coconut oil for cooking
Replace butter with olive oil in a suitable recipe
Replace canola oil with butter in a suitable recipe
Replace a nut spread with a butter-based spread
quizQuestions.answer: Replace butter with olive oil in a suitable recipe
quizQuestions.explanation: Replacing saturated or trans fats with mono- or polyunsaturated fats can improve the overall fat pattern; dietary fat remains an essential nutrient.

quizQuestions.question: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?
options: Vitamins A, B12, C, and E
Vitamins B1, B6, B12, and C
Vitamins A, C, D, and B12
Vitamins A, D, E, and K
quizQuestions.answer: Vitamins A, D, E, and K
quizQuestions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in body fat and require dietary fat for absorption; B vitamins and C are water-soluble.

quizQuestions.question: Vitamin C deficiency causes which disease?
options: Beriberi
Scurvy
Rickets
Pellagra
quizQuestions.answer: Scurvy
quizQuestions.explanation: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency, causing collagen breakdown, bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and fatigue.

quizQuestions.question: Why are vitamins A, D, E, and K grouped together?
options: They dissolve mainly in water
They supply energy like fats
They dissolve mainly in fats
They are amino-acid compounds
quizQuestions.answer: They dissolve mainly in fats
quizQuestions.explanation: These vitamins dissolve in fat and can be stored in the body more readily than water-soluble vitamins.

quizQuestions.question: Which food is a useful source of vitamin C?
options: A serving of unfortified brown rice
A serving of cooked chicken breast
A serving of fresh bell pepper
A serving of plain cooked pasta
quizQuestions.answer: A serving of fresh bell pepper
quizQuestions.explanation: Many fruits and vegetables, including citrus fruit and bell peppers, provide vitamin C.

quizQuestions.question: Which structural role is a major function of calcium?
options: Binding oxygen within hemoglobin
Helping mineralize growing bones and teeth
Helping form iodine-containing thyroid hormones
Serving as the main extracellular fluid electrolyte
quizQuestions.answer: Helping mineralize growing bones and teeth
quizQuestions.explanation: Calcium is a major structural mineral in bones and teeth. Iron is central to hemoglobin, iodine is part of thyroid hormones, and sodium is the main extracellular fluid electrolyte.

quizQuestions.question: Untreated or sufficiently severe iron deficiency can progress to which condition?
options: Vitamin B12-deficiency anemia
Folate-deficiency anemia
Anemia from acute blood loss
Iron-deficiency anemia
quizQuestions.answer: Iron-deficiency anemia
quizQuestions.explanation: Iron deficiency can exist before anemia develops. If iron stores remain too low, hemoglobin production can fall and iron-deficiency anemia can result.

quizQuestions.question: Which listed choice is a common calcium-rich food source?
options: Unfortified rice-based beverage
Unfortified apple juice drink
Calcium-fortified soy beverage
Unfortified oat-based beverage
quizQuestions.answer: Calcium-fortified soy beverage
quizQuestions.explanation: Dairy foods and fortified soy beverages can provide substantial calcium; labels and dietary needs still matter, and many other calcium sources exist.

quizQuestions.question: What is the role of iron in hemoglobin?
options: Binding oxygen for transport in the blood
Forming clots after blood vessel injury
Recognizing pathogens to trigger an immune response
Regulating blood glucose after a carbohydrate-rich meal
quizQuestions.answer: Binding oxygen for transport in the blood
quizQuestions.explanation: Iron in hemoglobin binds oxygen so red blood cells can transport it. Clotting, pathogen recognition, and blood-glucose regulation involve different components and processes.

quizQuestions.question: What health concern is associated with consistently excessive sodium intake?
quizQuestions.answer: Consistently excessive sodium intake is associated with higher blood pressure and increased cardiovascular risk, although individual needs and medical advice can vary.
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong answer links sodium with blood-pressure regulation without treating one food or one day as a diagnosis.

quizQuestions.question: Why does the percentage of water in the human body vary among people?
options: Age and body composition affect the proportion
A universal percentage applies after early childhood
Total body weight sets the proportion
Short-term thirst gives the exact body-water percentage
quizQuestions.answer: Age and body composition affect the proportion
quizQuestions.explanation: Body-water percentage varies across infancy, adolescence, adulthood, and different body compositions, so one fixed percentage should not be applied to everyone.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an early sign of dehydration?
options: Frequent pale urine and little thirst
A lower resting pulse and improved alertness
A feeling of hunger and increased saliva
Dark yellow urine and increased thirst
quizQuestions.answer: Dark yellow urine and increased thirst
quizQuestions.explanation: Thirst and darker yellow urine can suggest dehydration, especially after fluid loss, but neither is a diagnosis. Foods, supplements, medicines, and health conditions can also affect urine color.

quizQuestions.question: Why is urine color only one clue, rather than a perfect test, of hydration?
options: Urine color mainly measures how recently a person exercised
Urine color directly measures total water in the body
Foods, medicines, and health factors can also change color
Urine color reflects daily water intake regardless of context
quizQuestions.answer: Foods, medicines, and health factors can also change color
quizQuestions.explanation: Hydration assessment uses context and multiple signs; urine color can be influenced by factors besides fluid intake.

quizQuestions.question: Which beverage is usually the best everyday choice for hydration, and why?
quizQuestions.answer: Plain water is usually the best everyday hydration choice because it replaces fluid without added sugar; individual needs can vary with activity, climate, and health.
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong answer identifies water and explains why special drinks are not generally needed for routine hydration.

quizQuestions.question: Over time, energy balance broadly compares:
options: Energy intake compared with use for growth, activity, and body functions
Food energy compared with energy used during deliberate exercise alone
Nutrient intake compared with a standard calorie target for the age group
Food consumed today compared with activity completed on the same day
quizQuestions.answer: Energy intake compared with use for growth, activity, and body functions
quizQuestions.explanation: Energy balance is a broad accounting concept. In adolescents, growth, development, body regulation, illness, and measurement error mean it should not be treated as a precise daily equation or a guarantee of stable weight.

quizQuestions.question: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) refers to:
options: Energy consumed through food and beverages
Energy used at rest for vital body functions
Energy used for digesting and absorbing meals
Energy used during planned physical exercise
quizQuestions.answer: Energy used at rest for vital body functions
quizQuestions.explanation: BMR is the number of calories the body burns at rest to maintain basic physiological functions like breathing and circulation.

quizQuestions.question: A teenager is worried about weight and plans a severe calorie restriction. What is the safest next step?
options: Use a popular adult diet as the starting point for restriction
Set a lower intake target and check growth concerns later
Discuss concerns with a trusted adult and qualified clinician
Follow a peer’s calorie plan before deciding about adult help
quizQuestions.answer: Discuss concerns with a trusted adult and qualified clinician
quizQuestions.explanation: Teenagers are still growing; individualized concerns should be discussed with trusted adults and qualified professionals rather than addressed through crash diets.

quizQuestions.question: Which factor can change BMR itself, rather than describing intake or a separate component of daily energy expenditure?
options: The energy used to digest a particular meal
Changes in age, body composition, and growth
The pace of one afternoon’s exercise session
The nutrient values printed on a food package
quizQuestions.answer: Changes in age, body composition, and growth
quizQuestions.explanation: BMR varies with factors such as age, body size and composition, growth, hormones, and health.

questions.question: Which of the six nutrient classes provides 9 calories per gram?
options: Carbohydrates
Vitamins
Protein
Fat
questions.answer: Fat
questions.explanation: Fat provides 9 calories per gram — more than twice the energy density of carbohydrates or protein (4 cal/g each).

questions.question: What does the glycemic index compare under standardized conditions?
options: Nutrient density relative to each food’s energy content
Fiber content of customary equal-weight food portions
Carbohydrate amounts in customary serving portions
Glucose responses to matched carbohydrate portions
questions.answer: Glucose responses to matched carbohydrate portions
questions.explanation: The glycemic index compares glucose responses using standardized available-carbohydrate portions; glycemic load, serving size, preparation, and overall food quality are separate considerations.

questions.question: What defines a complete protein?
options: All nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions
More total protein than any incomplete protein source
Amino acids supplied exclusively through animal foods
Essential amino acids made from nonessential amino acids
questions.answer: All nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions
questions.explanation: Complete proteins supply all nine essential amino acids the body cannot make on its own.

questions.question: Why are trans fats considered especially harmful in nutrition education?
options: They lower both LDL and HDL, reducing energy available to tissues
They raise HDL alone, increasing cholesterol removal from tissues
They lower LDL alone, limiting cholesterol delivery to tissues
They raise LDL and lower HDL, increasing cardiovascular risk
questions.answer: They raise LDL and lower HDL, increasing cardiovascular risk
questions.explanation: Public health guidance generally recommends limiting trans fats because of their effect on blood cholesterol and cardiovascular risk.

questions.question: Which vitamin group is stored more readily in body fat than water-soluble vitamins?
options: A, D, E, and K
A, B12, C, and E
B1, B6, B12, and C
A, C, D, and B12
questions.answer: A, D, E, and K
questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble, requiring dietary fat for absorption and stored in body fat.

questions.question: Untreated or sufficiently severe iron deficiency can lead to:
options: Vitamin B12-deficiency anemia
Folate-deficiency anemia
Iron-deficiency anemia
Anemia from acute blood loss
questions.answer: Iron-deficiency anemia
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency is not identical to anemia, but prolonged or severe deficiency can reduce hemoglobin and produce iron-deficiency anemia.

questions.question: Which is an early sign of dehydration?
questions.answer: Early signs of dehydration can include thirst, dry mouth, darker urine, fatigue, headache, or reduced concentration.
questions.explanation: A strong response names observable early warning signs and connects them to the need to replace fluids before dehydration becomes more serious.

questions.question: Which statement best describes energy balance over time?
options: Energy intake compared with use for growth, activity, and basic functions
Energy intake compared chiefly with use during structured physical exercise
Energy intake matched exactly to expenditure within each calendar day
Energy intake set by a standard target shared by each adolescent age group
questions.answer: Energy intake compared with use for growth, activity, and basic functions
questions.explanation: Energy balance is approximate and changes over time; adolescent growth and individual physiology make exact daily equality and universal targets inappropriate.

questions.question: Which choice best reflects current federal dietary guidance?
options: Choose meals mainly by front-of-package health claims
Choose meals mainly by the lowest possible calorie count
Choose varied nutrient-dense foods across food groups
Choose supplements before evaluating the overall meal pattern
questions.answer: Choose varied nutrient-dense foods across food groups
questions.explanation: Current guidance emphasizes nutrient-dense foods, variety, and reduced reliance on highly processed foods.

questions.question: When might a sports drink be useful instead of water alone?
options: During a short walk in mild weather
During prolonged exercise with heavy sweating
During a seated lesson in an air-conditioned classroom
During routine flexibility exercises with little sweating
questions.answer: During prolonged exercise with heavy sweating
questions.explanation: Water is usually sufficient for routine activity; prolonged vigorous exercise, heavy sweating, heat, and individual needs can change fluid and electrolyte needs.

questions.question: Which role is associated with omega-3 fatty acids?
options: Providing rapid fuel for sprints
Supporting heart and brain function
Serving as building blocks for muscle proteins
Storing glucose for rapid release during exercise
questions.answer: Supporting heart and brain function
questions.explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids help support cell membranes and normal heart and brain function. Carbohydrates are the main rapid fuel for high-intensity activity, amino acids form proteins, and glycogen stores glucose.

questions.question: Which description best identifies a complete protein food?
options: Supplies all nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions
Provides enough total protein regardless of amino-acid balance
Provides amino acids from animal foods rather than plant foods
Provides a higher energy density than incomplete protein foods
questions.answer: Supplies all nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions
questions.explanation: A complete protein supplies all nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions. Total protein quantity, energy density, or animal origin alone does not define completeness; some plant foods also provide complete protein.

questions.question: Which benefit is associated with dietary fiber?
options: Supplying rapidly absorbed glucose for intense exercise
Supporting bowel function and helping regulate blood glucose
Supplying amino acids for growth and repair of muscle
Carrying fat-soluble vitamins across the intestinal wall
questions.answer: Supporting bowel function and helping regulate blood glucose
questions.explanation: Dietary fiber supports bowel function. Depending on fiber type and the overall diet, it can also support satiety, cholesterol management, and blood-glucose regulation.

questions.question: Why is there no single daily fluid target that fits every active teenager?
questions.answer: Fluid needs vary with age, body size, activity intensity and duration, climate, diet, health, and sweat rate. A strong answer names several factors and explains that thirst and other signs provide context.
questions.explanation: Hydration guidance should account for individual and environmental differences rather than use one universal cup target.

questions.question: Calcium is most important during adolescence for:
options: Increasing oxygen transport in blood
Supplying the main electrolyte lost through sweat
Supporting bone mineral accumulation
Supporting the production of thyroid hormones
questions.answer: Supporting bone mineral accumulation
questions.explanation: Adolescence is the critical window for peak bone mass development; adequate calcium intake during this period reduces lifelong osteoporosis risk.

questions.question: Which meal best applies current federal guidance to a student's lunch?
options: Vegetables, fruit, brown rice, and beans with water
White bread, processed meat, chips, and a sweetened drink
A sweetened cereal bar, fruit punch, and refined crackers
Refined pasta, a pastry, and a soft drink
questions.answer: Vegetables, fruit, brown rice, and beans with water
questions.explanation: A varied nutrient-dense meal supplies several nutrient classes and supports sustainable eating patterns.

questions.question: Which action best supports a healthy relationship with food during adolescence?
options: Choose meals chiefly by calorie count
Change meals chiefly to match an influencer’s body-size goals
Eat regular balanced meals and seek qualified guidance
Adjust intake chiefly to compensate for yesterday’s foods
questions.answer: Eat regular balanced meals and seek qualified guidance
questions.explanation: Growth-supporting habits and individualized professional guidance are safer than restrictive, appearance-driven plans.

questions.question: Why can two teenagers have different energy needs?
options: Growth, body composition, activity, and health can differ
Age alone provides a complete estimate of energy needs
School grade provides a consistent target for both students
Activity levels matter but growth differences can be ignored
questions.answer: Growth, body composition, activity, and health can differ
questions.explanation: Energy needs are individualized and reflect several biological and activity factors.

questions.question: Which meal best applies nutrient-density and variety guidance?
options: Vegetables, brown rice, beans, and water
Refined crackers, a bar, and soda
White bread, processed meat, and fruit punch
Refined cereal, a pastry, and a sweetened drink
questions.answer: Vegetables, brown rice, beans, and water
questions.explanation: Nutrient-dense patterns emphasize variety across food groups and beverages with little added sugar; the exact foods can vary by culture, access, preference, and health needs.

questions.question: Which change would most directly lower saturated-fat intake while preserving a source of dietary fat?
options: Replace olive oil with coconut oil for cooking
Replace butter with olive oil in a suitable recipe
Replace canola oil with butter in a suitable recipe
Replace nuts with a similar portion of full-fat cheese
questions.answer: Replace butter with olive oil in a suitable recipe
questions.explanation: Replacing a saturated fat with an unsaturated fat can improve the overall fat pattern.

questions.question: Which nutrient is uniquely produced by the body through sunlight exposure?
questions.answer: Vitamin D is the nutrient the body can produce when ultraviolet rays from sunlight reach the skin.
questions.explanation: Vitamin D can also come from foods or supplements, but this question focuses on the body's ability to synthesize vitamin D through sun exposure.

questions.question: After a long, vigorous practice, which snack best combines carbohydrate and protein?
options: Fruit with plain water
Pretzels with applesauce
Rice cakes with jam
Yogurt with fresh fruit
questions.answer: Yogurt with fresh fruit
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate helps replenish fuel and protein supports repair; individual needs vary with the activity and athlete.

questions.question: A student compares two breakfasts. Which evidence best supports the more nutrient-dense choice?
options: It carries a prominent wellness claim
It supplies fiber, protein, vitamins, and minerals
It has fewer calories regardless of the nutrient amounts
It has fewer ingredients regardless of the nutrient amounts
questions.answer: It supplies fiber, protein, vitamins, and minerals
questions.explanation: Nutrient density compares useful nutrients with the overall food and eating pattern, not marketing alone.

questions.question: On a Nutrition Facts label, which section helps compare how much a nutrient contributes to a daily reference amount?
options: Serving size
Total grams listed for one nutrient
Calories per serving
Percent Daily Value
questions.answer: Percent Daily Value
questions.explanation: Percent Daily Value helps compare nutrient amounts across foods using a standard daily reference; individual needs may differ.

questions.question: A student has a one-hour routine practice in mild weather. Which hydration plan is usually appropriate?
options: Drink water before, during as needed, and after practice
Wait until practice ends before replacing fluid losses
Choose a caffeinated energy drink for routine hydration
Use concentrated sports drinks despite limited sweating
questions.answer: Drink water before, during as needed, and after practice
questions.explanation: For routine activity, water and attention to thirst and conditions are generally appropriate.

questions.question: Which mineral is especially important for building bone during adolescence?
options: Iron
Sodium
Calcium
Zinc
questions.answer: Calcium
questions.explanation: Adolescence is an important period for bone development, and calcium is a major bone mineral.

questions.question: Ingredients on a U.S. food label are listed in what order?
options: By the amount of each nutrient supplied
By ingredient weight, greatest to least
By alphabetical order of ingredient names
By ingredient weight, least to greatest
questions.answer: By ingredient weight, greatest to least
questions.explanation: Ingredient lists place the ingredient used in the greatest amount by weight first.

questions.question: Explain one way dietary fiber supports health.
questions.answer: Dietary fiber supports digestive regularity and can contribute to satiety, blood-glucose regulation, and heart health depending on the fiber and overall diet.
questions.explanation: A strong response accurately explains at least one function and connects it to a fiber-rich food or eating pattern.

questions.question: Which pattern is a warning sign that a teenager may need support from a trusted adult or health professional?
options: Choosing a preferred food as part of varied meals
Trying unfamiliar foods while retaining familiar choices
Repeated severe restriction or distress about eating
Selecting water to drink with regular balanced meals
questions.answer: Repeated severe restriction or distress about eating
questions.explanation: Persistent restrictive behavior or distress around food deserves timely, supportive adult and professional attention.

questions.question: Which pattern helps explain the cardiovascular benefits associated with a Mediterranean-style diet?
options: Frequent refined grains with little fiber
Frequent use of butter and fatty red meats as staples
An emphasis on fruit juice rather than whole plant foods
Frequent plant foods and unsaturated fats
questions.answer: Frequent plant foods and unsaturated fats
questions.explanation: Mediterranean-style patterns commonly emphasize vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts, and olive oil. Benefits are associated with the overall pattern rather than a single food guaranteeing an outcome.

questions.question: Which listed nutrient has the highest caloric density?
options: Fat (9 cal/g)
Protein (4 cal/g)
Water (0 cal/g)
Carbohydrate (4 cal/g)
questions.answer: Fat (9 cal/g)
questions.explanation: Fat provides 9 calories per gram, the highest energy density of any macronutrient.

questions.question: Severe vitamin C deficiency can lead to which condition?
options: Beriberi
Rickets
Scurvy
Pellagra
questions.answer: Scurvy
questions.explanation: Severe vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy. Beriberi involves thiamine deficiency, pellagra involves niacin deficiency, and rickets commonly involves vitamin D deficiency or problems with bone mineralization.

questions.question: A teenager is considering a crash diet promoted online. Which response best applies this course?
options: Copy an adult calorie target from social media
Discuss growth-supporting habits with qualified support
Begin the restrictive plan and seek guidance if symptoms appear
Compare online testimonials before choosing a rapid weight-loss plan
questions.answer: Discuss growth-supporting habits with qualified support
questions.explanation: Teenagers are still growing, so severe restriction and generic online targets can be unsafe. Qualified support can account for growth, health, access, culture, and individual needs.

questions.question: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) represents:
options: Energy used during vigorous physical exercise
Energy used across an entire day of activity
Energy consumed through a typical daily diet
Energy used at rest for vital body functions
questions.answer: Energy used at rest for vital body functions
questions.explanation: BMR is the rate of energy use under standardized resting conditions needed to support basic functions such as breathing and circulation; it is only one component of total daily energy needs.

questions.question: Sodium's excessive intake is most associated with increased risk of:
questions.answer: Excessive sodium intake is most associated with increased risk of high blood pressure, which can raise risk for heart disease and stroke.
questions.explanation: This answer identifies the direct health concern, high blood pressure, and connects it to broader cardiovascular risk.
